entities.name: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884) is a picaresque novel by American author Mark Twain, widely considered one of the greatest American novels and a foundational text of American literature. Published in the United Kingdom in December 1884 and the United States in February 1885, it is a sequel to The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876) and follows the runaway boy Huck Finn and the escaped slave Jim as they travel down the Mississippi River on a raft.

The novel's central moral drama is Huck's gradual recognition that Jim is a full human being despite Huck's upbringing in a slave-holding society. In the famous Chapter 31, Huck tears up the letter that would return Jim to slavery and says 'All right, then, I'll go to hell' — a moment Ernest Hemingway identified as the origin of all American literature. Twain's use of regional dialect, first-person colloquial narration, and satirical treatment of Southern society made the novel formally revolutionary as well as morally significant.

The book has been simultaneously celebrated as an anti-racist masterpiece and critiqued for its use of racial epithets and its portrayal of Jim. It has been banned or challenged more often than almost any other novel in US history. Its influence on American literature is incalculable: Hemingway declared 'All modern American literature comes from one book by Mark Twain called Huckleberry Finn,' and it shaped the tradition of first-person vernacular narration that runs through J.D. Salinger, Ralph Ellison, and beyond.
